analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare to negotiate prices for excessively priced life-sustaining drugs, benchmarked to five other countries.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in November 2019 with zero cosponsors, referred to two House committees, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have the Department of Health and Human Services review all life-sustaining prescription drugs every year and flag any priced more than 10% above the average price in Canada, the UK, Germany, France, and Japan. For drugs flagged as excessively priced, the Secretary would be required to negotiate prices for Medicare's prescription drug benefit, with steep financial penalties for manufacturers that refuse to agree to a price. Drug makers would also have to report prices, revenues, research spending, and advertising spending for these drugs publicly, and any person could petition HHS to review a drug's price.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries and taxpayers who pay for the Medicare prescription drug benefit would gain if the bill passed, because the government would negotiate down the prices of life-sustaining drugs rather than accept manufacturers' listed prices. The public database of excessive price determinations would also give patients and doctors visibility into which drugs cost far more in the U.S. than abroad.

how_it_helps.text: HHS would review all life-sustaining drugs at least annually and determine whether each price is excessive, using an international benchmark: a price exceeding 110% of the average price in Canada, the UK, Germany, France, and Japan is automatically excessive. [S2] [S3]

For drugs determined to be excessively priced, the Secretary would be required to negotiate the payment Medicare drug plans may make, capped at 110% of the international reference price — replacing the current law (struck by Section 3) that bars Medicare from negotiating drug prices. [S3] [S2]

Manufacturers that refuse to negotiate would face civil penalties reaching a large share of their U.S. sales revenue for the drug, with penalty collections deposited into the Medicare Hospital Insurance Trust Fund. [S3]

The bill would create a public database of excessive price determinations and require manufacturers to report prices, revenues, R&D and advertising spending for these drugs, subject to daily civil penalties for failing to report. [S2] [S3]
Any person could petition HHS to make an excessive price determination for a drug, with the petition, documentation, and the Secretary's rationale made public. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers selling life-sustaining drugs in the U.S. would bear the cost, through lower negotiated Medicare prices capped at international levels and through penalties and mandatory disclosure of their pricing, research, and marketing finances. Some of that cost could be shifted toward higher prices for non-Medicare customers or somewhat less revenue available for R&D and marketing.

drawbacks.text: The bill covers only 'life-sustaining' drugs under Medicare Part D, so most other overpriced prescription drugs would remain untouched by the negotiation mandate. [S3] [S2]

The international reference price cap penalizes manufacturers when pricing data is thin: for drugs lacking an international reference price, penalties scale to 50–95% of U.S. sales revenue until an agreement is reached, a blunt instrument that critics of reference pricing argue could discourage development of new life-sustaining therapies or reduce their availability. [S3]

The mechanism depends on pricing information from foreign countries; the bill itself acknowledges some drugs would lack reference-country data, forcing HHS to rely on a more discretionary 'reasonable price' analysis that could invite inconsistent determinations and litigation. [S3] [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Medicare beneficiaries, the benefit is substantial: negotiated prices capped near what other wealthy countries pay for life-sustaining drugs, plus public disclosure of manufacturers' research and marketing spending. The cost falls almost entirely on brand-name drug manufacturers, and the risk that reduced revenue slows development of new therapies is real but modest for already-marketed drugs. The main design weakness is scope — it addresses only life-sustaining drugs — but within that scope it directly targets the best-documented gap between U.S. and foreign drug prices.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees — later the Health subcommittee — for its entire life; no hearing, no markup, no vote ever happened before the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Daniel Lipinski introduced the bill on November 12, 2019, and it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and, in addition, the Ways and Means Committee. [S1] [S5]
The next day, November 13, 2019, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, the furthest it progressed. [S5]
The action history shows no further activity of any kind after November 14, 2019, through the end of the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off because the bill died: Medicare would have been required to negotiate their life-sustaining drug prices down to roughly what the same drugs cost in Canada, the UK, Germany, France, and Japan, with penalties reaching most of their U.S. sales revenue for noncompliance. No manufacturer faces those price caps or the mandated public disclosure of research and marketing finances.

for.name: Rep. Daniel Lipinski
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it

against.name: House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees
against.what_they_did: Received the referral but never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill died in committee

against.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers
against.what_they_did: The industry has long opposed international reference pricing and Medicare price negotiation, the two mechanisms this bill would impose

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no partisan split was recorded; it had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: The bill would cap their Medicare prices at roughly 110% of what the same drugs cost in five other countries, force public disclosure of their research and marketing spending, and impose revenue-based penalties for refusing to negotiate. The industry's U.S. pricing — typically far above international levels — is the direct target.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D prescription drug plans and Medicare Advantage insurers
industries.note: Insurers that run Medicare drug plans would pay less for excessively priced life-sustaining drugs, reducing their costs. Lower negotiated prices would also reduce what beneficiaries pay out of pocket.
Manufacturers would have to report total marketing and advertising expenditures for each life-sustaining drug annually, subject to penalties for noncompliance, increasing scrutiny of drug promotion.
